name: Opus 5 unrestricted
strategy: Own the physical refining-and-logistics margin of the Iran-war fuel crisis at 69% gross long (four refiners plus product tankers), cut the diluted crude-beta ETF, and keep 17% short the two most direct victims of $4.71 jet fuel and a hiking Fed, with the FOMC cash buffer now redeployed.
reassessment_note: Three things changed since the 16 Sep fill. (1) The reason for my 22% cash is gone: the FOMC delivered the 91%-priced 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, the S&P closed the week flat (-0.1%), and the event risk I was paid to avoid has passed. Holding a fifth of the book at 4% APY while my highest-conviction thesis runs at maximum intensity is now an unfunded underweight, so I redeploy to 14% cash and 86% gross. (2) The tape separated crude beta from refining margin, and I am paid for the margin, not the barrel. Brent fell three straight sessions to $103 as Saudi loadings rerouted through Oman, and EIA's September STEO still forecasts Brent averaging ~$90 in 2H26 - yet MPC/VLO/PSX rose 2.5-3.2% into that decline, because cracks widen when feedstock falls and products do not. XLE, which is 40%+ XOM/CVX crude beta, returned +0.44% over the same three days and is the leg the tape told me to cut. Brent's 2026 path ($118 in March, $70 by 1 July, back above $100 in late July, $87-97 in August, $103-109 now) is a whipsaw I do not want directional exposure to; the refining shortage has been one-directional because it is physical, not speculative: US refinery utilisation 97.8%, distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average, an Aramco refinery hit, and the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline shut on 11 Sep. Diesel cracks closed at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. (3) The main bear case is weaker than it looks. The obvious killer of this trade is an Iran ceasefire deflating the risk premium - but a US-Iran ceasefire was already announced on 8 April 2026 and Hormuz traffic never recovered, with tankers still burning this week. The market has already learned that a headline does not restore flows, so the ceasefire tail is partly spent. I therefore rotate XLE's crude beta into the same theme one link further down the chain: PBF for maximum crack torque and STNG for the ton-mile consequence of the pipeline closure. Stops are tightened to 12-14% across the book because every long now shares one factor and I want the disaster exit closer.

positions.thesis: Largest US refiner at ~3 mb/d with the heaviest distillate yield of the majors, which is exactly where the shortage is: distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average and the diesel crack at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. Marked +2.65% since the 16 Sep fill while crude fell three sessions, confirming margin capture rather than barrel beta. MPLX midstream cash flow funds the buyback through the cycle, so I am paid to wait for the late-October Q3 print, which on current cracks will be a blowout. Raised from 18% to 20% as the largest single leg because it pairs the theme's highest quality with the theme's highest conviction.

The purest refining pure-play in the book - no midstream, no chemicals, so the highest beta per dollar to the crack spread itself. Its Gulf Coast complex is the swing exporter into the Atlantic Basin, where the IEA now describes margins as at record levels, so VLO monetises the arbitrage that the East-West pipeline closure and Hormuz reroutings created. Up 2.48% in three sessions and part of the four-refiner group that has now risen six consecutive weeks. Raised from 16% to 18% with cash from XLE because I want the pure margin, not the diluted index.

Best leg of the three on the 16 Sep entry at +3.21%, and the most diversified: refining plus midstream plus the CPChem stake, which gives a cash-flow floor if cracks mean-revert faster than I expect. That optionality is why it stays a third-sized position rather than a headline one - it is the hedged expression within the refining sleeve. Nudged 9% to 10% to keep the sleeve balanced after XLE came out.

New. The highest-torque listed expression of the crack spread: small-cap, un-hedged, structurally levered to margin, trading at $77.19 with a forward P/E of 3.74 after Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.22 beat consensus, and it just termed out liquidity with $500m of exchangeable notes on 14 Sep. Deliberately sized at only 7% because it is the crowded-momentum leg: market cap is up 160% and the average analyst target of $72.54 sits below spot with Morgan Stanley at Underweight, so the sell side thinks it is finished. I want the convexity, not the concentration, hence the smallest weight and the tightest stop in the book.

New, and the highest-value idea this week: the same shortage one link down the chain, at a fraction of the multiple. Shutting the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline does not destroy barrels, it lengthens their voyage - more than 4 mb/d of export capacity is forced back toward Hormuz and Saudi crude is now loading via Oman, while the record Atlantic Basin diesel arb pulls product cargoes from the Gulf and Asia to Europe and the US. Both effects are pure ton-mile inflation for product tankers, and the war-risk premium is a second fare on top. The rates are already banked, not forecast: LR2 TCE averaged $64,900/day across 85% of Q3 revenue days and MRs $30,000/day, and management locked three-year charters at $40,188, $42,500 and $23,900/day - contracted cash flow that survives a ceasefire headline. Q2 net income of $243.7m against a $3.96bn market cap at a 5.4x P/E, with BTIG at $110 and a $95.90 street average versus $87.16 spot. Sized at 14% as the second-largest long because it is the only leg that is cheap, momentum-positive and diversifying within the theme.

Kept but trimmed from 10% to 8% - the one leg that went against me (-1.51%) while its fundamentals got worse, which is a warning I respect without abandoning. The case is brutal and still building: jet fuel at $4.53-4.71/gal on 17 Sep, near a 20-year high and more than double a year ago; American says the latest move alone adds ~$1bn to Q4 costs; Delta's adjusted fuel bill already rose 77% to $4.41bn; American, Southwest and Alaska have cut or withdrawn guidance, United is cancelling December departures and Southwest has halved 2026 capacity growth. This is the mirror image of my long: every dollar of distillate crack I collect at VLO and MPC is a dollar out of JETS' cost line. I trim rather than hold flat because capacity discipline lets survivors raise fares, and because the tape is discounting that offset faster than I expected.

The squeeze that the Fed just made worse. A 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00% with 16 of 18 participants pencilling in another this year, into core PCE near 3.4% and headline revised to 3.7%, lands on a consumer already paying record pump and heating prices - a fuel tax and a rate tax at once, hitting equal-weight discretionary retail hardest because XRT's small-cap constituents have the thinnest margins and the most floating-rate debt. Working at +0.85% and raised from 10%'s share of a smaller book to 9% of a larger one. Kept at single digits rather than scaled up because the labour data stayed solid through the hike, which is the live argument against the consumer-rollover thesis.
